title: Two ways of remembering
hook: in the Pali texts Kassapa is the strict forest elder; in Zen he is the one who smiled when the Buddha held up a flower (SN 16; Gateless Gate, case 6)

segments.voice: Yesterday, dana, and your line: he ate it. Did you use one gift, not just thank someone for it? Today, the same Kassapa, remembered in two very different ways. Day seven hundred forty-three.

A crowd on a mountain, waiting for a talk. The teacher comes, sits, and says nothing at all. He just holds up a flower. The whole gathering stays silent. And then one monk smiles. That's the scene a Zen collection called the Gateless Gate sets down, and the monk who smiles is Mahakassapa. The same man we've spent this week with: the one in rag robes, eating alone by a wall. Two pictures of one person. Today we hold them side by side.
screen: `A CROWD WAITING FOR A TALK.` → `A FLOWER, HELD UP.` → `ONE MONK SMILES.`

segments.voice: First, the elder of the Pali texts. In the chapter of discourses gathered around him, Kassapa is the forest monk who wants little and keeps the strict practices into old age. He can be blunt: asked by the Buddha to teach the monks, he says they have grown hard to speak to, and reports two of them competing over who can talk the most. And when the Buddha dies, it's Kassapa who calls the elders together to make sure the teaching survives. Second, the smiler of Zen. In the Gateless Gate, after Kassapa smiles, the Buddha speaks. In paraphrase: I have the treasury of the true dharma eye, a teaching that doesn't rest on words, and I entrust it to Mahakassapa. Zen tradition remembers this as the teaching passing to Kassapa, not as a speech but as a glance, from mind to mind. Third, how the two fit. The flower story belongs to Zen; it isn't told in the Pali discourses. Theravada Buddhists remember Kassapa through the suttas and their commentaries. Zen Buddhists remember him through this silent moment, and many other stories too. Neither memory needs the other to be wrong. And look closer: both are about a man who doesn't need much. A forest, a worn robe, a bowl of rice. Or a flower, and no words at all. Fourth, why it matters. Love for someone can hold more than one picture of them. A grandmother who was strict with her children and soft with her grandchildren. A friend who's loud at parties and quiet at a hospital bed. Both are true. Both are her. Both are him.
screen: `THE STRICT FOREST ELDER.` · `THE ONE WHO SMILED.` · `TWO MEMORIES, ONE SIMPLE MAN.` · `PEOPLE CARRY MANY PICTURES.` · then, large: `BOTH ARE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two stories at once. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you know well, living or gone. Find one picture of them that's stern, or difficult, or serious. Then find another that's tender, or funny, or surprising. Set the two side by side in your mind. Don't make one cancel the other. Don't decide which one is the real person. Just let both be true, and breathe with them for a while. The bell holds the time.
Mahakassapa. The name both traditions remember him by: the strict forest elder of the Pali texts and the one who smiled at the flower in Zen. Today's word.

Your line: both are him. Today, when someone surprises you by acting unlike the person you thought they were, let the new picture sit beside the old one, and keep them both. Day seven hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists honor Mahakassapa as the forest elder of the suttas; Zen and Chan lineages name Mahakassapa as the first ancestor after the Buddha, and teachers retell the flower story.

fork.setup: you're in the crowd on the mountain. the teacher sits down, holds up a flower, and says nothing. what do you do?
options: wait politely for the talk to start.
ask a neighbor what it means.
fork.reveal: in the Gateless Gate, Kassapa smiles, and the Buddha says he entrusts his wordless teaching to him.

original.note: Pali Mahakassapa, great Kassapa: the name both traditions remember him by (Sanskrit Mahakashyapa).

trapdoor: what you thought: two different monks with the same name.
what it means: one man, remembered as a strict forest elder in the Pali texts and as the one who smiled in Zen.
what a scholar hears: the flower story is told in the Gateless Gate (case 6) and other Chan and Zen sources, not in the Pali canon.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 16 (Kassapa Samyutta, the discourses on Kassapa)
Wumenguan (The Gateless Gate), case 6: the World-Honored One holds up a flower

notes: No date given for the Gateless Gate, per the claims rule. The case is paraphrased: confirm the Buddha at Vulture Peak holds up a flower, the assembly is silent, only Kassapa smiles, and the Buddha speaks of the 'treasury of the true dharma eye' and entrusts it to Mahakassapa.

'The flower story isn't told in the Pali discourses' and 'Zen lineages place Kassapa at the head of their line of teachers after the Buddha': confirm both, and that the framing is fair to Theravada and Zen alike.
'He rebukes monks who talk too much and practice too little': loosely based on SN 16.6–16.8; confirm or soften.
The council is mentioned in one sentence only; day 744 tells it.

Editor: fixed the ambiguous 'the Buddha says that he has the treasury' (read as if Kassapa had it) into a clear paraphrase of the Buddha's words; cut hook embellishments not in case 6 ('old monk', people looking at each other) for 'the whole gathering stays silent'; replaced the unsourced lineage-chart claim with 'Zen tradition remembers this as the teaching passing to Kassapa'; tied 'blunt' to SN 16.6 (two monks competing at talking); review line updated to match day 742's revised carry.

Auditor (serious): in SN 16.6 it is the Buddha, not Kassapa, who summons and rebukes the two competing monks (Bhanda and Abhinjika); Kassapa only declines to exhort and reports them. Teach corrected. howItsDone's 'lineage charts' softened; confirm.
